current_episode.title: ConPulse | Secrets to grow your E-commerce brand in the USA with Jennifer Alexander

guest.bio_context: Jennifer Alexander has 20 to 25 years of experience spanning B2B e-commerce, direct-to-consumer, e-retail, and back to B2B. She worked at Johnson & Johnson in vision care and consumer division (now Kenvue), as well as Estée Lauder in prestige beauty. She started her career as a consultant for an Internet startup, working on e-commerce projects including building a prototype for a fashion brand before cloud systems were available. Recently, she has returned to the consulting business after leaving the corporate world.

pending_qa.q: How should e-commerce brands understand product pricing and consumer buying behavior across different product categories?
pending_qa.r: High-end lipstick might retail for $18 while low-end costs $2-3, creating very different unit economics and shipping strategies. An impulse buy like a low-cost lipstick requires different handling than an expensive moisturizer or electronic device, which typically require multiple visits, research, and visits to competing sites before purchase. Understanding this consumer journey and buying lifecycle is fundamentally critical to building authentic brand experiences.

pending_qa.q: What marketing spend allocation framework should e-commerce brands use to balance stability and innovation?
pending_qa.r: Jennifer Alexander uses the 70-20-10 framework originally from Google: spend 70% of advertising budget on core work projects that drive the majority of your business, 20% on related initiatives, and 10% on testing new channels. For most e-commerce brands, the 70% typically goes to paid search, retargeting ads, and email, while the remaining 30% tests product carousels, social ads, AI, payment options, and emerging technologies.

pending_qa.q: How do subscription and save programs perform in the U.S. e-commerce market?
pending_qa.r: Subscribe and save programs, like Amazon's famous offering, still only make up about 5% to 15% of total business depending on the category, and even for consumable products like dog food that people buy regularly, adoption remains low. U.S. consumers often prefer the choice and convenience of ordering when they want rather than committing to automatic recurring shipments.

pending_qa.q: What is the dominant payment method for U.S. online shoppers and what emerging payment options are gaining traction?
pending_qa.r: Credit cards still dominate as the primary payment method for U.S. e-commerce consumers. However, digital wallets like Apple Pay and Google Pay are increasingly popular, and split payment options like Affirm, which breaks payments into four installments, are also gaining adoption as alternative payment methods.
